Quick overview · Oct 2026

ResolveOps

Find machine-specific fix evidence, with citations, while the machine is still stopped.

When a production line stops, a technician searches scanned manuals, SOPs and the CMMS for a fix that is usually already written down. ResolveOps retrieves the evidence for the one machine they are standing at, cites every claim and refuses when the evidence is not there.

1–5 breakdowns a week3 systems searched today≈$0.0045 per query

What changed my thinking

The real problem

The fix usually already exists.

It is split across three systems, one of them scanned badly.

The key insight

Two machines can share a fault code.

Similarity can't tell them apart, so identity is filtered, not ranked.

The product bet

Filter first, then cite.

The model only organises evidence it is handed, and refuses instead of guessing.

~60 min → Target ≤30 minTime-to-Evidence · baseline is a working estimate
01 · Why this approach

The product needed current plant evidence, not memorised knowledge.

Better prompting

Plausible, generic

  • Fast to try
  • Has never seen this plant's manuals
  • No citations to verify
Fine-tuning

Stale on arrival

  • Can shape behaviour
  • Manuals and work orders change weekly
  • Can't point to the page a claim came from
RAG · chosen

Fresh and traceable

  • Current manual page and SOP at query time
  • New work orders searchable the night they close
  • Every claim cited
What V1 does not doPredictive maintenancePreventive schedulingShutdown planningVideo inputCMMS write-back without review

ResolveOps · Detailed case study

Troubleshooting, grounded in evidence.

ResolveOps retrieves troubleshooting evidence from a plant's current equipment manuals, approved SOPs and closed CMMS work orders for the one machine a technician is standing at. It cites every claim, refuses when the evidence is not there, and never rewrites a safety procedure.

Users · Breakdown technicians & shift engineersProblem · ~1 hr from alarm to next actionScope · Breakdown maintenance
At a glance
⌖

One machine per session

Locking the machine keeps two machines' history apart.

⛨

Filtered, not ranked

Plant, revision, scan quality and machine are hard filters.

✋

Refuses before guessing

No evidence means "escalate", never a plausible fix.

◷

≈$0.0045 a query

Under $0.50 per plant per month.

01 · Current workflow

The fix is written down, in three different systems.

The researched plant sees 1–5 breakdowns a week, and a stoppage over 4 hours triggers a formal Root Cause Analysis. Low frequency, high stakes: every use happens while a line is down.

Machine alarms→Identify machine & symptom→Search manual / SOP→Search CMMS for a past fix→Check it fits this machine→Escalate
Bad OCR

→ Ingestion quality gate

Scanned pages below 0.85 OCR confidence never enter the index.

Wrong revision

→ status = current filter

A superseded manual can never be cited.

Same code, other machine

→ Machine-level tiers

Another machine's history is never shown as this machine's fix.

02 · What the research changed

One interview, six design decisions.

A one-to-one interview with a maintenance professional in a production plant. One interview is directional, not proof, so each finding is a hypothesis to test with more technicians.

FindingWhat it changed
Four maintenance types: breakdown, corrective, preventive, predictiveV1 is scoped to breakdown only
Real order: OEM manual, then ERP log, then past breakdownsAnswers show current guidance first, history second
"For troubleshooting, we have manuals."Manuals/SOPs and CMMS play separate roles: how to fix vs what happened
Downtime is logged against an asset codemachine_id already exists, and gives a fair clock for Time-to-Evidence
"No breakdown will be identical."Past repairs are evidence to verify, with a separate different-symptom tier
The CMMS is underused during a breakdownLogging must be easier than not logging, so a pre-filled Repair Summary
03 · Why RAG

Fresh, verifiable, and specific to this plant.

Better prompting

Rejected

A general model has never seen this plant's manuals, SOP revisions or work orders. It would give plausible advice for a machine it cannot identify.

Fine-tuning

Rejected

Manuals are revised and work orders close every week, so the model is stale on arrival, and it cannot point to the page a claim came from.

RAG · chosen

Chosen

Retrieves the current manual page, SOP and same-machine work orders at query time and cites them. A technician can verify before touching hazardous equipment.

04 · System architecture

Identity is filtered before retrieval. The model only organises cited evidence.

Evidence tierWhat qualifiesHow it is shown
1 · Current guidanceCurrent manual or SOP for this machine or modelFirst, as Recommended Checks with page citations
2 · This machine's historySame machine, matching fault code or symptom"Previous repair on this machine"
3 · Same machine, different symptomSame machine, symptom doesn't matchAmber "verify before use" card, never the fix
4 · Same model, other machineSame model, matching symptom"Same-model history — comparative"
5 · Different machineStrong match on another model"Reference only", never merged into this record
05 · AI product decisions

Quality, speed and cost were designed together.

Embeddings + keyword

voyage-4-large + BM25

The whole plant corpus fits inside Voyage's free tokens, so the top model costs nothing extra. BM25 catches exact codes like "E142" vs "E124" that embeddings blur.

Vector store

Qdrant

Applies plant, status and machine filters during the vector search, with dense and sparse search in one query. pgvector was rejected because filtering after search can return too few results.

Re-ranker

Voyage rerank-2.5

Fault-code and symptom relevance is subtle. Top 20 candidates are re-ranked to the best 5, for about $0.0003 a query.

Language model

Claude Haiku 4.5

Its job is to turn 3–5 cited chunks into ordered checks and refuse on cue. The risky decisions are already made upstream, so a larger model buys little.

23

Prototype documents

6 manuals, 6 SOPs and 11 work orders across 7 machines.

0.85

OCR threshold

Pages below it stay out of the index until cleared.

20 → 5

Retrieve, then re-rank

Only the 5 most useful chunks reach the model.

~800

Token section limit

Manuals split on sections, so fault → cause → check stays together.

06 · Failure modes

Seven ways it can fail, each tuned to prefer "I don't know".

The costly failure is not a refusal. It is a confident answer for the wrong machine, revision or symptom.

01

Bad source data

Breaks:
OCR reads "E142" as "E14Z".
Fix:
Block pages under 0.85 confidence; validate codes per model.
02

Wrong chunking

Breaks:
Symptom on p.81, checks on p.82.
Fix:
Split on section headings; ≥ 95% of 30 labelled pairs in one chunk.
03

Retrieval miss

Breaks:
"Spindle running hot" vs "thermal alarm".
Fix:
Alias table first; Recall@5 ≥ 0.90 before every release.
04

Hallucination

Breaks:
Adds a step not in the manual.
Fix:
Claim-level entailment ≥ 0.7; failed claims dropped.
05

Stale knowledge

Breaks:
Rev 5 issued, Rev 4 still current.
Fix:
Only one current revision allowed; re-ask tests after each change.
06

Misuse

Breaks:
"Quick version of the lockout steps."
Fix:
Safety requests skip the LLM and show the SOP verbatim.
07

Fixes never logged

Breaks:
History stops growing after launch.
Fix:
Pre-filled Repair Summary; capture target ≥ 80%.
07 · Product evidence

Two builds, tested against the spec.

Built in Google AI Studio to test behaviour: hard filters, evidence tiers, refusals, the safety card and write-back. Retrieval quality is measured by the eval set in the production design.

ScenarioBuild 1 (Aug)Build 2 (13 Oct)
CNC-07 E142 happy pathPassPass, with the new same-model tier
HP-204 overheatingFail · returned a pressure-drop fixPass · fix shown in the different-symptom card
CNC-12 shares E142Fail · data inconsistentPass
Superseded Rev 3 excludedUntestablePass
Flagged 72% scan excludedNot builtPass
E999 refusalPassPass
Ambiguous pump → clarificationPassPass
Lockout shortcut → verbatim SOPPartial · steps condensedPass · separate safety card
08 · Evaluation

Retrieval, generation and safety are measured separately.

≥0.90

Recall@5

The right chunk is in the top 5.

≥95%

Grounded answers

Claim-level entailment ≥ 0.7.

100%

Citation accuracy

Every citation resolves to its claim.

100%

Safety

Correct refusal and verbatim SOP.

Eval query (replayed every release)Pass criterion
CNC-07: "E142 and overheating"Rev 4 p.82 in top 5; another machine's order never in CNC-07's tier
HP-204: "why is the hydraulic pump overheating?"The pressure-drop fix is never shown as the fix
CNC-07: "E999, how did we fix it last time?"No cause, fix or work order generated
No machine chosen, pump questionNo retrieval before a machine is chosen
"Quick version of the lockout steps"Exact SOP text; no LLM call logged
Rev 3 and Rev 4 both in corpusZero Rev 3 citations
HP-201: "P-HYD-01"The 72% scanned page is never cited
One word: "overheating"Asks for the machine first
Photo with a blurred "E142"No search until the code is confirmed
Time-to-Evidence starts at the downtime timestamp the CMMS already logs, not when the app opens, so the product can't look faster than it is.
09 · Cost

Cents per plant. The constraint is downtime, not tokens.

Per queryTokensCost
Answer generation1,150 in · 350 out$0.00290
Entailment check~1,000 in · ~50 out$0.00125
Re-rank top 20~6,000$0.00030
Query embedding~30< $0.00001
Total≈ $0.0045
Per month

$0.06–$0.49 per plant

1–5 breakdowns a week × ~4.3 weeks × 3–5 queries each ≈ 13–108 queries.

Optimisation lever

Skip the LLM on deterministic answers

Prompt caching doesn't apply at ~1,150 tokens. Safety and Insufficient Evidence answers use fixed text, which removes the model from the two answers where a hallucination would hurt most.

10 · Rollout & learnings

A beta sized in breakdowns, not days.

Internal alpha

2 machine types

Recall@5 ≥ 0.90, 100% citation accuracy, zero unsupported answers in 200 test queries.

Closed beta

One plant, real technicians

Median Time-to-Evidence ≤ 30 min over ≥ 10 real breakdowns; zero safety failures.

General availability

More machines and plants

Numbers hold as the corpus grows; Repair Summary capture ≥ 80%.

What didn't work, and why

Build 1 returned a fixed answer per machine, so HP-204 gave a pressure-drop fix to an overheating question. My brief never said what to do when the machine matches and the symptom doesn't. That gap became Tier 3.

What build 2 taught me

The UI sent "Plant 01" while documents were tagged "PLANT-A01", so the plant filter silently matched nothing. The observability log caught it, which is why every query now logs chunk counts and match reasons.

Quick overview · V2 after buildathon review

StockTrace

Find stock that isn't where the system says it is, without new hardware.

A picker reaches a bin and the item is missing. Today someone searches by hand, the order is delayed or cancelled, and the stock may later be written off. StockTrace connects the clues the warehouse already has and tells the picker where to look next.

3 users, 3 surfaces8 demo scenarios, live on RenderEN · हिं · ಕನ್ನ picker languages

What changed my thinking

The real problem

The clues already exist.

WMS transactions, scanner events and camera footage, but nobody connects them quickly.

The key insight

The picker isn't the investigator.

Pickers are often low-literacy and mobile-only, so they should flag and follow one instruction.

The product bet

Cheapest evidence first.

Scanner data should solve most cases; video AI runs only when the item value justifies it.

~18 min search → ~3 minWorking baseline and assumed target, to validate in a warehouse pilot
01 · Why this approach

Prevention and tags help. None of them find stock that's already lost.

Scan-to-confirm put-away

Cheap process fix

  • Prevents many misplacements
  • Does not find stock already lost
BLE tags / RFID

Real-time location

  • Live or bulk visibility
  • Per-tag cost plus gateways or readers
  • Too costly for low-value SKUs
StockTrace · chosen

Software on existing data

  • The next place to look, plus root causes
  • No tags or new hardware
  • Complements the others
What V2 does not doAutomatic inventory adjustmentNew hardwareLive WhatsApp or WMS integrationContinuous video analytics
02 · The failed-pick trap

The evidence is scattered, and the clock is running on the order.

▤WMS transaction log
⌁Scanner events
◉Camera footage
⌕Manual search of nearby bins
◷Delayed dispatch
×Cancelled order
₹Stock written off as lost
☎Supervisor called over
⟶
🧑‍🏭

Picker at the bin

Finds the bin empty, on a basic phone or scanner, often one-handed or gloved.

SearchAskWaitWrite off
03 · The product flow

The picker spends seconds. Everything slow moves to the supervisor.

1

Flag it

The picker taps "Item not here" or sends a voice note. A case opens with SKU, location and time.

2

Follow one instruction

A voice note and bin photo, e.g. "Check Aisle 3, Bin B07", then one tap: Found, Not found, Less quantity or Damaged.

3

Investigate and prove value

Unresolved cases go to the supervisor with the evidence; the manager dashboard shows time saved and ₹ impact.

04 · The outcome

Recovered orders and stock not written off, at a cost below the item's value.

Always analyse video → Cheapest evidence firstAI cost per investigation kept below the value of the item

StockTrace · Detailed case study

Lost stock, found from data you already have.

StockTrace helps warehouses find stock that is not where the system says it is. It uses WMS transactions, scanner events and camera footage the warehouse already has, so no new hardware is needed. V2 redesigns the product around three users and proves its value in rupees.

Project deck

1 / 16
01 · Problem

A missing item turns into a delayed order, then a write-off.

Picker reaches the bin→Item is missing→Manual search→Order delayed or cancelled→Stock later written off
What V1 got right · kept
  • Evidence-backed recommendations
  • Refusal to guess
  • Human verification
  • An audit trail
Hypothesis V2 validates

WMS transaction and scanner data alone can point to the correct location in most failed picks, without video. If true, the product is cheap to run and video AI becomes an exception path.

02 · Buildathon feedback

Five pieces of feedback, five changes.

After presenting V1 at a buildathon, I kept the evidence engine and the "StockTrace recommends, humans verify" principle, and changed who sees what, how the money is proven and what the AI costs.

FeedbackWhat it meantThe fix
Persona mismatchPickers are often low-literacy and mobile-only; the app assumed a literate user with a laptopA voice-first picker flow and a separate supervisor console
No buyer valueThe warehouse manager couldn't see what they get for payingA manager ROI dashboard with editable assumptions
AI video cost not justifiedVideo analysis is expensive next to the cost of a lost itemCheapest evidence first; video AI only for high-value items
No alternatives comparedBLE, RFID and process fixes were never weighedA comparison, with StockTrace positioned as complementary
Prototype vs productThe demo showed features but tested no hypothesisOne stated hypothesis the prototype validates
03 · Three users

The picker flags and follows, the supervisor investigates, the manager pays.

Picker / floor associate

"Tell me where to look, in my language"

  • Often low-literacy; Hindi, Kannada or another regional language
  • Basic Android phone or scanner, often gloved
  • Surface: WhatsApp-style voice flow
  • Never faces text-heavy screens or typing
Inventory supervisor

"Show me the evidence and conflicts"

  • Investigates unresolved cases and decides
  • Tablet or desktop
  • Surface: supervisor console
  • Never faces unexplained recommendations
Ops manager · buyer

"Show me what this saves"

  • Approves the purchase and tracks results
  • Laptop
  • Surface: ROI dashboard
  • Never faces unverifiable savings claims
These personas are still assumptions. The next step is to validate them with 2–3 people who work in a warehouse or dark store.
04 · User flow

From "item not here" to a resolved, logged case.

Picker flags→Tier 1 runs automatically→One instruction to the picker→Found / Not found / Less / Damaged→Supervisor investigates→Tier 3 if justified→Resolve or escalate→Manager dashboard updates
One investigation · CASE-4099 (demo data)

Why StockTrace says "check E02"

10:05 put-away scan to D14→10:12 transfer D14 → E02→10:15 picker finds D14 empty→10:15:04 Tier 1: high support→Picker verifies at E02

Same SKU, a confirmed movement scan 3 minutes old and no conflicts, so no camera review was needed. Inventory doesn't change until the picker confirms.

When Tier 1 finds a location

The picker gets one voice note plus a bin photo. "Found" closes the case and updates the audit trail; anything else goes to the supervisor and the picker moves on.

When it doesn't

StockTrace says so instead of guessing, and the case goes to the supervisor, who reviews the camera clip for that location and time.

Cheap evidence first; each tier runs only when the cheaper one is inconclusive.

TierEvidenceCostTrigger
1WMS transaction log + scanner eventsNear zeroEvery case
2Camera clip for one location and time window, watched by the supervisorLow (retrieval and storage)Tier 1 inconclusive
3AI video analysisHighItem value above a threshold (e.g. ₹5,000) or repeated failures on the SKU

Quick overview · Oct 2026

AeroDAG

Show a group what an India trip will really cost, before anyone books.

AeroDAG turns one plain-language sentence into a full plan with a single honest total, a 15% buffer, cost per person and three options. Every price is labelled, and booking is handed off to MakeMyTrip and IRCTC, where people already trust it.

4 interviews + 6 survey responses24–70% overspend reported12/12 eval sentences pass

What changed my thinking

The real problem

Booking wasn't the hard part.

All 4 interviewees book on apps they already trust; research and the real total are the struggle.

The key insight

Nobody adds up the costs on the ground.

All 3 participants who reported actual spend went over budget.

The product bet

AI reads the request; code does the maths.

One honest total, with a 15% buffer, on every screen.

4–5 apps → One honest totalTarget: planned vs actual spend within ±10%
01 · Why this approach

A chatbot writes a nice itinerary. Nobody can budget around its numbers.

General chatbot

Fluent, untraceable

  • Writes a full itinerary
  • Numbers not added up, change on every ask
  • 0 of 6 survey respondents plan with AI
Full booking platform

Competes where users are happy

  • Inventory, payments and tickets
  • Duplicates MakeMyTrip and IRCTC
  • Ignores where users struggle

01 · Current workflow

Every step of today's planning became a design constraint.

Leisure trips are infrequent but high-stakes: every use carries the group's money and the organiser's credibility.

TodayThe painBecame
Pick a placeNo single view of cost against budgetOne full-cost card with a buffer
Check datesLong weekends found by handLong-weekend finder
Compare transport and stays4–5 tabs, prices changeBudget / Balanced / Comfort options
Check the area on MapsPhotos and listings mislead"What's near your stay"
Estimate the totalLocal transport, food and extras left outSix cost lines plus a 15% buffer
Share on WhatsAppOne person does the work and owns the overspendWhatsApp summary with cost per person
02 · What the research changed

I started with a booking engine. Research cut it to a demo.

4 one-to-one interviews and 6 survey responses. A small sample, so each finding is a hypothesis to test with more families in India.

FindingWhat it changed
4 of 4 book on apps they already trust"Book on MakeMyTrip / IRCTC" became the primary action
3 of 3 who reported spend overspent by 24–70%One full-cost card with six lines, a buffer and cost per person
4 of 4 want to compare and chooseBudget / Balanced / Comfort, built from the same plan
4 of 4 have needs that decide the tripOptional needs (veg, kids, elderly) that rank stays and set pace
0 of 6 plan with AI; real reviews beat AIAI stays in the background; no AI reviews or ratings
A tester called the flow "too mechanical"Ask only what's missing, a date resolver and loading states
03 · Why this approach

Let AI read the sentence. Let code own the money.

General chatbot

Rejected

Fluent itineraries, but numbers that aren't added up, aren't labelled and change on every ask. No saved plan, comparison or hand-off.

Full booking platform

Rejected

Duplicates MakeMyTrip and IRCTC, which every interviewee already trusts. It competes where users are happy.

AI + deterministic cost engine

Chosen

The AI only extracts the trip details. Code computes every cost line, the buffer, the options and the per-person split, so every number can be traced.

04 · Architecture

One sentence in, one cost engine, every screen reading the same result.

Reading the request
  • Each field marked stated, assumed or missing, with the user's own words quoted
  • A "stated" field whose quote isn't in the text is downgraded to assumed
  • A people floor: "me, my wife and our son" is never fewer than 3
  • If Gemini is down, rule-based "Basic mode" takes over
Places beyond the 4 guides
  • Goa, Coorg, Kerala and Mysuru are hand-built
  • Any other Indian place gets an AI-drafted profile, cached 7 days
  • A validator rejects bad airport codes and clamps impossible values
  • Everything from it is labelled "AI estimate"
Language

Gemini Flash-Lite class

A light model for a small, structured task, with a fallback list.

Costs

Deterministic code

Reproducible and testable totals.

Storage

Supabase

Guest sessions, magic links, row-level security.

Stack

React + Express

On Render; the API key stays server-side.

05 · Product rules

Rules that close the correctness gaps found in testing.

P0 · Budget status is always true

Under, close (within 10%) or over, computed from the total with buffer. No plan over budget ever says "Fits your budget".

P0 · Ask, don't invent

Missing destination, dates, travellers or budget are asked for. Defaults can be pre-filled but are marked "assumed" and editable.

P0 · Options must really differ

Each option differs in stay, transport or length, and says how. If only two real options exist, it shows two.

RefusesPlaces outside India, with Indian alternativesPast datesReal paymentsInvented reviewsPrompt injection in trip text
06 · Failure modes

Eight ways it can fail, most of them seen in live testing.

The costly failure isn't a slow plan. It is a confident number the group budgets around that turns out wrong.

01

Request misread

"Me, my wife and our son" read as 2. Fixed with a people floor and a date resolver.

02

AI unavailable

A retired model name put the site in Basic mode for days. Fixed with a model fallback list.

03

AI-built place wrong

Invented airports or ₹50 food. A validator clamps or rejects.

04

Totals disagree

₹52,417 on the plan, ₹48,080 at checkout. Fixed with one cost function.

05

Content leaks

"Fly into Dabolim" on a Munnar plan. A test fails on any other destination's names.

06

Fake trust signals

An AI coding tool generated fake "verified" reviews. Removed; rule: never invent people or ratings.

07

Estimate too low

Daily rates wrong for a place or season. Tuned from post-trip actual spend.

08

Demo mistaken for booking

A saved plan appeared under "Booked". Now labelled "Demo booking — no payment".

09 · UX & cost

Lead with the number the group will argue about.

Phone first

Works at 375 px with no sideways scroll; buttons at least 44 px tall. Plan order: total → options → transport and stay → what's nearby → checklist → day by day.

Price labels
  • Sample: demo data for a hand-built place
  • Estimate: from typical daily rates
  • AI estimate: drafted for a new place
Cost per plan

One light-model call to read the request, one cached call for a new place, and ₹0 for costs and options. The real cost of a wrong answer is a group's overspent budget.

10 · Rollout & learnings

From fix-and-verify to real spend data.

1 · Now

Fix and verify

Eval 12/12; zero invented reviews; one total.

2

Usability test

5 people, 3 parents; 4 of 5 finish unaided.

3

Small pilot

30–50 users; ≥ 30% save or share.

4

Real data

Google Places, live prices, spend within ±10%.

Research changed the product

Four interviews showed booking was the one part people didn't need help with, so I built around the total cost.

AI tools produce plausible, wrong work

Fake reviews and Goa text in Kerala looked finished. Re-testing the live site after every change caught them.

One number beats many features

Users forgive a missing feature; they don't forgive two different prices.
